newsitem.title: USA: US House panel to restore food safety chief funds.
newsitem.headline: US House panel to restore food safety chief funds.

text.p: House appropriators will restore funding for a top-level U.S. Agriculture Department food safety position this week following a personal appeal by Secretary Dan Glickman. a senior aide said on Monday.
In June, the House Appropriations subcommittee on agriculture chose not to fund the undersecretary position, which was created when Congress reorganized the agriculture department in 1994.
"We were kind of just taking a shot at them," for being slow to fill the position, a senior subcommittee aide told Reuters. "We'll put the money back in."

Congress created the undersecretary slot in recognition of USDA's growing role in food safety issues, especially after several children in Washington state died in early 1992 from eating hamburgers tainted with the e. coli bacteria.
President Clinton's first choice for the food safety post was Mike Taylor, a former director of the Office of Seafood at the Food and Drug Administration.
However, Taylor's nomination was never sent to the Senate because controversy over some decisions he made at FDA made it unlikely he would be confirmed, congresional aides said.
Taylor served as acting undersecretary for food safety until November 1996, when he returned to the private sector.
Six months later, Clinton nominated current USDA Deputy Undersecretary for Research, Education and Economics Catherine Wotecki to the food safety post.
However, by the time the House Appropriations subcommittee on agriculture met on June 25, Wotecki's nomination papers still hadn't been sent to the Senate.
To "poke" the administration into action, the panel decided not to fund the undersecretary slot, the aide said.
That prompted Glickman to send a letter urging the panel to reverse its decision. "This is very important to me," he said.
The Clinton administration also finally sent Wotecki's nomination papers to the Senate Agriculture Committee over the weekend, a committee spokeswoman said Monday.

That should clear the way for an easy confirmation process -- assuming funding is restored as expected when the full House Appropriations Committee mets Wednesday on the fiscal 1998 agriculture spending bill.
